title: P, NP, NP-Hard and Undecidable, in Plain English
oneLiner: What the complexity classes mean, reductions and why some problems are NP-hard, the pseudo-polynomial knapsack trick, what to do with an NP-hard problem, and the halting problem.
keyTakeaway: P is problems solvable quickly; NP is problems whose answers are quick to check. NP-complete problems are the hardest in NP, all equally hard, and nobody knows a fast algorithm for any of them. Reductions prove hardness by turning one problem into another. Knapsack's O(n*W) DP is pseudo-polynomial, exponential in the input's length. Some problems, like the halting problem, no algorithm can solve.
explanation:
Big O says how fast an algorithm is; complexity classes ask how fast any algorithm for a problem could be. This lesson keeps it informal: P, NP, NP-complete and NP-hard, what a reduction is, and why a small change in the rules moves a problem from easy to impossibly hard.

It covers the knapsack 'isn't that polynomial?' trick, the practical options when a problem is NP-hard, and the halting problem, the classic example of something no program can decide.
